claim: GTP-tubulin is preferentially incorporated at growing microtubule ends.
source: GTP-tubulin is preferentially incorporated at growing microtubule ends, but the biochemical mechanism by which the bound nucleotide regulates the strength of tubulin:tubulin interactions is debated.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact in the field.

claim: The 'self-acting' (cis) model posits that the nucleotide (GTP or GDP) bound to a particular tubulin dictates how strongly that tubulin interacts.
source: The 'self-acting' (cis) model posits that the nucleotide (GTP or GDP) bound to a particular tubulin dictates how strongly that tubulin interacts, whereas the 'interface-acting' (trans) model posits that the nucleotide at the interface of two tubulin dimers is the determinant.
evidence: This is a definition of the self-acting model provided in the abstract.

claim: The 'interface-acting' (trans) model posits that the nucleotide at the interface of two tubulin dimers is the determinant of interaction strength.
source: The 'self-acting' (cis) model posits that the nucleotide (GTP or GDP) bound to a particular tubulin dictates how strongly that tubulin interacts, whereas the 'interface-acting' (trans) model posits that the nucleotide at the interface of two tubulin dimers is the determinant.
evidence: This is a definition of the interface-acting model provided in the abstract.

claim: With a self-acting nucleotide, plus- and minus-end growth rates decreased in the same proportion to the amount of GDP-tubulin in simulations.
source: with a self-acting nucleotide, plus- and minus-end growth rates decreased in the same proportion to the amount of GDP-tubulin, whereas with interface-acting nucleotide, plus-end growth rates decreased disproportionately.
evidence: This is a result from computational simulations described in the abstract.

claim: With interface-acting nucleotide, plus-end growth rates decreased disproportionately compared to minus-end growth rates in simulations.
source: with a self-acting nucleotide, plus- and minus-end growth rates decreased in the same proportion to the amount of GDP-tubulin, whereas with interface-acting nucleotide, plus-end growth rates decreased disproportionately.
evidence: This is a result from computational simulations described in the abstract.

claim: Experimental measurements showed a disproportionate effect of GDP-tubulin on plus-end growth rates compared to minus-end growth rates.
source: We then experimentally measured plus- and minus-end elongation rates in mixed nucleotides and observed a disproportionate effect of GDP-tubulin on plus-end growth rates.
evidence: This is an experimental result reported in the abstract.

claim: GDP-tubulin binds at and 'poisons' plus-ends but not at minus-ends.
source: Simulations of microtubule growth were consistent with GDP-tubulin binding at and 'poisoning' plus-ends but not at minus-ends.
evidence: This is a conclusion from simulations described in the abstract.

claim: Nucleotide exchange at terminal plus-end subunits mitigates the poisoning effect of GDP-tubulin.
source: Quantitative agreement between simulations and experiments required nucleotide exchange at terminal plus-end subunits to mitigate the poisoning effect of GDP-tubulin there.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing simulations to experiments, described in the abstract.

claim: The interfacial nucleotide determines tubulin:tubulin interaction strength.
source: Our results indicate that the interfacial nucleotide determines tubulin:tubulin interaction strength, thereby settling a longstanding debate over the effect of nucleotide state on microtubule dynamics.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract.

claim: Microtubules grow by the addition of GTP-bound tubulin to the polymer ends.
source: Microtubules grow by the addition of GTP-bound tubulin to the polymer ends.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Once incorporated into the microtubule lattice, tubulins hydrolyze their bound GTP.
source: Once incorporated into the microtubule lattice, tubulins hydrolyze their bound GTP.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The change in nucleotide state triggers conformational changes that weaken interactions between neighboring tubulins and ultimately results in catastrophe.
source: The change in nucleotide state triggers conformational changes that weaken interactions between neighboring tubulins and ultimately results in catastrophe, the switch from growth to shrinkage (Bowne-Anderson et al., 2013; Gudimchuk and McIntosh, 2021; LaFrance et al., 2022; Manka and Moores, 2018; Roostalu et al., 2020; Seetapun et al., 2012; Zanic et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: An early model posited that GTP-tubulin would form strong lattice contacts because GTP favors a 'straight' conformation compatible with the microtubule lattice.
source: An early model explained the nucleotide-dependence of microtubule stability by positing that nucleotide state determines the conformation of tubulin: GTP-tubulin would form strong lattice contacts because GTP favors a 'straight' conformation compatible with the microtubule lattice, and GDP-tubulin would form weak lattice contacts because GDP favors a 'curved' conformation incompatible with the microtubule lattice (Drechsel and Kirschner, 1994; Howard and Timasheff, 1986; Melki et al., 1989; Nicholson et al., 1999; Shearwin et al., 1994; Tran et al., 1997; Wang and Nogales, 2005).
evidence: This is a historical model supported by multiple citations.

claim: GDP-tubulin would form weak lattice contacts because GDP favors a 'curved' conformation incompatible with the microtubule lattice according to an early model.
source: An early model explained the nucleotide-dependence of microtubule stability by positing that nucleotide state determines the conformation of tubulin: GTP-tubulin would form strong lattice contacts because GTP favors a 'straight' conformation compatible with the microtubule lattice, and GDP-tubulin would form weak lattice contacts because GDP favors a 'curved' conformation incompatible with the microtubule lattice (Drechsel and Kirschner, 1994; Howard and Timasheff, 1986; Melki et al., 1989; Nicholson et al., 1999; Shearwin et al., 1994; Tran et al., 1997; Wang and Nogales, 2005).
evidence: This is a historical model supported by multiple citations.

claim: Both GTP- and GDP-tubulin adopt the same curved conformation.
source: However, subsequent work demonstrated that both GTP- and GDP-tubulin adopt the same curved conformation (Nawrotek et al., 2011; Pecqueur et al., 2012; Rice et al., 2008), which contradicted a core assumption of the cis-acting model.
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: The nucleotide binding site on β-tubulin forms part of the polymerization interface with the α-tubulin from the next subunit in the protofilament.
source: The 'trans' mechanism is supported by the knowledge that the nucleotide binding site on β-tubulin forms part of the polymerization interface with the α-tubulin from the next subunit in the protofilament, and it is also consistent with the largest nucleotide-dependent conformational changes in the microtubule occurring in α-tubulin adjacent to the β-tubulin-bound nucleotide (Alushin et al., 2014; Manka and Moores, 2018; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: The largest nucleotide-dependent conformational changes in the microtubule occur in α-tubulin adjacent to the β-tubulin-bound nucleotide.
source: The 'trans' mechanism is supported by the knowledge that the nucleotide binding site on β-tubulin forms part of the polymerization interface with the α-tubulin from the next subunit in the protofilament, and it is also consistent with the largest nucleotide-dependent conformational changes in the microtubule occurring in α-tubulin adjacent to the β-tubulin-bound nucleotide (Alushin et al., 2014; Manka and Moores, 2018; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to cryo-EM studies.

claim: Microtubule plus-ends present a β-tubulin polymerization interface that contains the exchangeable nucleotide.
source: Microtubule plus- and minus-ends are structurally distinct: plus-ends present a β-tubulin polymerization interface that contains the exchangeable nucleotide, whereas minus-ends present an α-tubulin polymerization interface that does not expose a nucleotide.
evidence: This is stated as established structural knowledge.

claim: Microtubule minus-ends present an α-tubulin polymerization interface that does not expose a nucleotide.
source: Microtubule plus- and minus-ends are structurally distinct: plus-ends present a β-tubulin polymerization interface that contains the exchangeable nucleotide, whereas minus-ends present an α-tubulin polymerization interface that does not expose a nucleotide.
evidence: This is stated as established structural knowledge.

claim: At the plus-end, two nucleotides could in principle be dictating the strength of lattice contacts: one bound to the terminal tubulin (the cis nucleotide), and one at the interface between the terminal tubulin and the next subunit in the microtubule lattice (the trans nucleotide).
source: Debate over cis- and trans-acting mechanisms (reviewed in Gudimchuk and McIntosh, 2021) has persisted in part because most studies have focused solely on the plus-end, where two nucleotides – one bound to the terminal tubulin (the cis nucleotide), and one at the interface between the terminal tubulin and the next subunit in the microtubule lattice (the trans nucleotide) – could in principle be dictating the strength of lattice contacts.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the structural arrangement at the plus-end.

claim: At the minus-end, the exchangeable nucleotide of the terminal tubulin is already buried in the microtubule lattice.
source: At the minus-end, by contrast, the exchangeable nucleotide of the terminal tubulin is already buried in the microtubule lattice.
evidence: This is stated as a structural fact about the minus-end.

claim: In the self-acting model, GDP-tubulin inhibited plus- and minus-ended growth to the same extent in simulations.
source: These simulations revealed a striking difference between the two mechanisms of nucleotide action: in the self-acting model, GDP-tubulin inhibited plus- and minus-ended growth to the same extent, but in the interface-acting model, GDP-tubulin disproportionately inhibited plus-ended growth.
evidence: This is a result from computational simulations.

claim: In the interface-acting model, GDP-tubulin disproportionately inhibited plus-ended growth in simulations.
source: These simulations revealed a striking difference between the two mechanisms of nucleotide action: in the self-acting model, GDP-tubulin inhibited plus- and minus-ended growth to the same extent, but in the interface-acting model, GDP-tubulin disproportionately inhibited plus-ended growth.
evidence: This is a result from computational simulations.

claim: An earlier study showed a selective suppression of plus-end elongation when GDP was included in the reaction mixture.
source: This observation was consistent with an earlier study that showed a selective suppression of plus-end elongation when GDP was included in the reaction mixture (Tanaka-Takiguchi et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Plus-end growth showed a roughly two-fold higher apparent on-rate constant than minus-end growth (3 µM–1 s–1 MT–1 and 1.5 µM–1 s–1 MT–1, respectively).
source: Both ends showed the same apparent critical concentration (Ccapp) of 50 nM, but plus-end growth showed a roughly two-fold higher apparent on-rate constant (konapp) than minus-end growth, 3 µM–1 s–1 MT–1 and 1.5 µM–1 s–1 MT–1, respectively (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an experimental measurement shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Both plus- and minus-ends showed the same apparent critical concentration (Ccapp) of 50 nM.
source: Both ends showed the same apparent critical concentration (Ccapp) of 50 nM, but plus-end growth showed a roughly two-fold higher apparent on-rate constant (konapp) than minus-end growth, 3 µM–1 s–1 MT–1 and 1.5 µM–1 s–1 MT–1, respectively (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an experimental measurement shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Growth rates at both ends decreased substantially in mixtures containing as little as 2.5% GDP (25 µM GDP and 975 µM GMPCPP).
source: Growth rates at both ends decreased substantially in mixtures containing as little as 2.5% GDP (25 µM GDP and 975 µM GMPCPP) (Figure 2C), but plus-end growth rates decreased to a greater degree than minus-end growth rates.
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Plus-end growth rates decreased to a greater degree than minus-end growth rates in mixed nucleotide experiments.
source: Growth rates at both ends decreased substantially in mixtures containing as little as 2.5% GDP (25 µM GDP and 975 µM GMPCPP) (Figure 2C), but plus-end growth rates decreased to a greater degree than minus-end growth rates.
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 2C.

claim: At 25 µM GDP, plus-end growth rates fell ~50% (from 2.2 nm/s to 1.1 nm/s) relative to 'all GMPCPP' growth rates.
source: For instance, at 25 µM GDP, plus-end growth rates fell ~50% (from 2.2 nm/s to 1.1 nm/s) relative to 'all GMPCPP' growth rates, whereas minus-end growth rates only fell ~30% (from 1 nm/s to 0.7 nm/s).
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental result.

claim: At 25 µM GDP, minus-end growth rates only fell ~30% (from 1 nm/s to 0.7 nm/s) relative to 'all GMPCPP' growth rates.
source: For instance, at 25 µM GDP, plus-end growth rates fell ~50% (from 2.2 nm/s to 1.1 nm/s) relative to 'all GMPCPP' growth rates, whereas minus-end growth rates only fell ~30% (from 1 nm/s to 0.7 nm/s).
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental result.

claim: The ~1.5-fold stronger inhibition by GDP of plus-end growth rates held across multiple nucleotide mixing ratios.
source: This ~1.5-fold stronger inhibition by GDP of plus-end growth rates held across multiple nucleotide mixing ratios (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Tubulin binds 12.5-fold less tightly to GMPCPP than to GDP.
source: The GMPCPP-tubulin concentrations that best recapitulate minus-end growth rates are consistent with tubulin binding 12.5-fold less tightly to GMPCPP (KDGMPCPP) than to GDP (KDGDP) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is inferred from fitting experimental data and supported by direct measurements.

claim: The inferred 12.5-fold difference in nucleotide binding affinities was supported by direct measurements of nucleotide binding.
source: This inferred difference of affinities was supported by direct measurements of nucleotide binding (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and agrees with prior reports (Correia et al., 1987; Hyman et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citations.

claim: Minus-end growth rates decreased stoichiometrically as the concentration of GDP-tubulin increased.
source: Minus-end growth rates decreased stoichiometrically as the concentration of GDP-tubulin increased, matching or even slightly exceeding the 'all GMPCPP' extrapolation.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the mixed nucleotide assays.

claim: Plus-end growth rates decreased super-stoichiometrically for a given concentration of GDP-tubulin.
source: In contrast, plus-end growth rates decreased super-stoichiometrically (were slower than expected based on the 'all GMPCPP' extrapolation) for a given concentration of GDP-tubulin (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The super-stoichiometric effect at the plus-end was most apparent when 25–55% of unpolymerized tubulin was bound to GDP.
source: This super-stoichiometric effect at the plus-end was observed over a range of GDP-tubulin concentrations, and was most apparent when 25–55% of unpolymerized tubulin was bound to GDP (Figure 3D inset).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 3D inset.

claim: The super-stoichiometric effect of GDP-tubulin on plus-end growth over a wide range of GDP-tubulin concentrations provides strong support for the interface-acting nucleotide mechanism.
source: The super-stoichiometric effect of GDP-tubulin on plus-end growth over a wide range of GDP-tubulin concentrations provides strong support for the interface-acting nucleotide mechanism.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The plus-end growth rates were recapitulated well using konplus of 0.74 µM–1 s–1, KDlongitudinal of 86 µM, and KDcorner of 25 nM.
source: The plus-end growth rates were recapitulated well using the same parameters obtained in a prior study (Cleary et al., 2022b; konplus of 0.74 µM–1 s–1, KDlongitudinal of 86 µM, KDcorner of 25 nM; Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a result from fitting simulations to experimental data, shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The minus-end-specific on-rate constant (konminus) was determined to be 0.31 µM–1 s–1.
source: To extend the model to fit the minus-end growth rates, we retained the same interaction affinities as for the plus-end (consistent with the equal apparent critical concentration at both ends, Figure 2B) and optimized a minus-end-specific on-rate constant. This procedure yielded a konminus of 0.31 µM–1 s–1 (Figure 4A), roughly 2-fold slower than the plus-end, which is in line with the ~twofold lower concentration-dependence of growth rates observed at the minus-end (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a result from fitting simulations to experimental data, shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Simulated minus-end growth rates decreased linearly as the concentration of GDP-tubulin increased, recapitulating the experimental measurements.
source: Simulated minus-end growth rates decreased linearly as the concentration of GDP-tubulin increased, recapitulating the experimental measurements (Figure 4B) and in agreement with our initial prediction using arbitrary parameters (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a result from simulations shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Simulated plus-end growth rates decreased super-stoichiometrically as the concentration of GDP-tubulin increased.
source: In contrast, simulated plus-end growth rates decreased super-stoichiometrically as the concentration of GDP-tubulin increased (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a result from simulations shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The model overpredicted the magnitude of the GDP-poisoning effect at the plus-end.
source: An outsized effect of GDP-tubulin at the plus-end is expected from the interface-acting mechanism, but the model overpredicted the magnitude of the effect.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing simulations to experiments.

claim: In the interface-acting nucleotide mechanism, the outsized effect of GDP at the plus-end occurs because GDP-tubulin can bind tightly to (and reside longer at) the plus-end if the interfacial nucleotide is GMPCPP.
source: In the interface-acting nucleotide mechanism, the outsized effect of GDP at the plus-end occurs because GDP-tubulin can bind tightly to (and reside longer at) the plus-end if the interfacial nucleotide is GMPCPP (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is an explanation of the mechanism illustrated in Figure 4D.

claim: The 'extended stay' of GDP-tubulin on the plus-end poisons the protofilament end against further growth and is the origin of the super-stoichiometric effect of GDP-tubulin at the plus-end.
source: This 'extended stay' of GDP-tubulin on the plus-end poisons the protofilament end against further growth and is the origin of the super-stoichiometric effect of GDP-tubulin at the plus-end (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is an explanation of the mechanism illustrated in Figure 4D.

claim: Faster rates of nucleotide exchange yielded smaller decreases in plus-end growth rates for a given concentration of GDP-tubulin in simulations.
source: Faster rates of nucleotide exchange yielded smaller decreases in plus-end growth rates for a given concentration of GDP-tubulin (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a result from simulations shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The rate of nucleotide exchange that best recapitulated the observed effects was 0.3–0.5 s–1.
source: The rate of nucleotide exchange that best recapitulated the observed effects was 0.3–0.5 s–1, which compares favorably to other estimates (Amayed et al., 2000; Melki et al., 1989; Yarbrough and Fishback, 1985; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from fitting simulations to experiments and is supported by citations.

claim: Microtubule plus- and minus-ends exhibit different sensitivities to GDP-tubulin, lending strong support for the interface-acting mechanism of nucleotide action.
source: In summary, using simulations and measurements of plus- and minus-end growth, we showed that microtubule plus- and minus-ends exhibit different sensitivities to GDP-tubulin, lending strong support for the interface-acting mechanism of nucleotide action.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the Results section.

claim: The outsized effect of GDP on plus-ends provides new insights into the fundamental mechanisms of microtubule dynamics.
source: The outsized effect of GDP on plus-ends provides new insights into the fundamental mechanisms of microtubule dynamics and adds to a growing body of evidence that suggests GDP-terminated protofilaments influence microtubule growth (Carlier and Pantaloni, 1978; Hamel et al., 1986; Valiron et al., 2010), fluctuations (Cleary et al., 2022b), catastrophe (Caplow and Shanks, 1996; Piedra et al., 2016), and regulation (Lawrence et al., 2022; Luo et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a conclusion supported by the current work and citations to prior work.

claim: GDP-terminated protofilaments influence microtubule growth, fluctuations, catastrophe, and regulation.
source: The outsized effect of GDP on plus-ends provides new insights into the fundamental mechanisms of microtubule dynamics and adds to a growing body of evidence that suggests GDP-terminated protofilaments influence microtubule growth (Carlier and Pantaloni, 1978; Hamel et al., 1986; Valiron et al., 2010), fluctuations (Cleary et al., 2022b), catastrophe (Caplow and Shanks, 1996; Piedra et al., 2016), and regulation (Lawrence et al., 2022; Luo et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Early views of the GTP cap did not anticipate the influence of GDP-tubulin on growing plus-ends.
source: Early views of the GTP cap did not anticipate the influence of GDP-tubulin on growing plus-ends, but there is now increasing evidence (Carlier and Pantaloni, 1978; Farmer and Zanic, 2023; Hamel et al., 1986; Margolin et al., 2012; Maurer et al., 2012; Roth et al., 2018; Valiron et al., 2010) that the cap is not 'all or nothing', and that GDP-tubulin can modulate microtubule growth without always initiating a catastrophe.
evidence: This is a statement about the historical development of the field.

claim: There is increasing evidence that the GTP cap is not 'all or nothing', and that GDP-tubulin can modulate microtubule growth without always initiating a catastrophe.
source: Early views of the GTP cap did not anticipate the influence of GDP-tubulin on growing plus-ends, but there is now increasing evidence (Carlier and Pantaloni, 1978; Farmer and Zanic, 2023; Hamel et al., 1986; Margolin et al., 2012; Maurer et al., 2012; Roth et al., 2018; Valiron et al., 2010) that the cap is not 'all or nothing', and that GDP-tubulin can modulate microtubule growth without always initiating a catastrophe.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent work.

claim: The tendency for plus-ended growth to 'stutter' and fluctuate might be explained by exposed GDP-tubulin.
source: Indeed, the tendency for plus-ended growth to 'stutter' (Mahserejian et al., 2022) and fluctuate (Cleary et al., 2022b) might be explained by exposed GDP-tubulin; exposed GDP-tubulin may also contribute to the higher frequency of catastrophe at the plus-end (Strothman et al., 2019; Walker et al., 1988).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Exposed GDP-tubulin may contribute to the higher frequency of catastrophe at the plus-end.
source: Indeed, the tendency for plus-ended growth to 'stutter' (Mahserejian et al., 2022) and fluctuate (Cleary et al., 2022b) might be explained by exposed GDP-tubulin; exposed GDP-tubulin may also contribute to the higher frequency of catastrophe at the plus-end (Strothman et al., 2019; Walker et al., 1988).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The work supports an emerging view of the growing microtubule end as a 'mosaic' of nucleotide states rather than a uniform assembly of GTP-tubulin.
source: Our work supports an emerging view of the growing microtubule end as a 'mosaic' of nucleotide states rather than a uniform assembly of GTP-tubulin (Brouhard and Sept, 2012; Brouhard and Rice, 2018; Cross, 2019; Duellberg et al., 2016; Farmer et al., 2021; Farmer and Zanic, 2023; Gudimchuk and McIntosh, 2021; Howard and Hyman, 2009; Margolin et al., 2012; Maurer et al., 2012; Roostalu et al., 2020; Roth et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a conclusion supported by the current work and multiple citations.

claim: The findings provide the most direct evidence to date in support of an interface-acting mechanism for nucleotide in microtubule stabilization.
source: In summary, the findings reported here provide the most direct evidence to date in support of an interface-acting mechanism for nucleotide in microtubule stabilization.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the Discussion section.

claim: The ATP binding site in AAA proteins resides at a protomer:protomer interface and dictates the geometry of oligomerization contacts.
source: Indeed, just as the GTP-binding site on β-tubulin forms part of the longitudinal interface between tubulin subunits, the ATP binding site in AAA proteins resides at a protomer:protomer interface and dictates the geometry of oligomerization contacts (Erzberger and Berger, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work on AAA proteins.

claim: For both AAA proteins and microtubules, residues important for nucleotide hydrolysis on one subunit are contributed by the next subunit in the oligomer or polymer.
source: Furthermore, for both AAA proteins and microtubules, residues important for nucleotide hydrolysis on one subunit are contributed by the next subunit in the oligomer or polymer (Banerjee et al., 2016; Brunger and DeLaBarre, 2003; Davies et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Similarities involving interfacial nucleotides in otherwise unrelated proteins may indicate a shared, convergently evolved mechanism for achieving force production in oligomers.
source: We speculate that these similarities involving interfacial nucleotides in otherwise unrelated proteins may indicate a shared, convergently evolved mechanism for achieving force production in oligomers.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the comparison between microtubules and AAA proteins.

claim: Simulated growth rates of GTP microtubule plus- and minus-ends were performed using arbitrarily chosen parameters that support elongation in the chosen concentration range.
source: Simulated growth rates of GTP microtubule plus- and minus-ends, using arbitrarily chosen parameters that support elongation in the chosen concentration range.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 1B and C.

claim: In a self-acting mechanism, both plus-end and minus-end growth rates are predicted to decrease linearly with the amount of GDP-tubulin.
source: In a self-acting mechanism, both plus-end (circles) and minus-end (squares) growth rates are predicted to decrease linearly with the amount of GDP-tubulin.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 1B and shown in the figure.

claim: In an interface-acting mechanism, plus-end growth rates are predicted to be disproportionately impacted by GDP-tubulin relative to minus-end growth rates.
source: In an interface-acting mechanism, plus-end (circles) growth rates are predicted to be disproportionately impacted by GDP-tubulin relative to minus-end growth rates.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 1C and shown in the figure.

claim: The predicted difference between self-acting and interface-acting mechanisms at the plus-end is robust across different choices for KDlong, KDcorner, and the GDP weakening effect.
source: The predicted difference between mechanisms at the plus-end is robust across different choices for KDlong, KDcorner, and the GDP weakening effect (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 1 and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: At 25 µM GDP, plus-end growth rates fell ~50% relative to 'all GMPCPP' growth rates, whereas minus-end growth rates only fell ~30%.
source: For instance, at 25 µM GDP, plus-end growth rates fell ~50% (from 2.2 nm/s to 1.1 nm/s) relative to 'all GMPCPP' growth rates, whereas minus-end growth rates only fell ~30% (from 1 nm/s to 0.7 nm/s).
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental result.

claim: Differences in the mean normalized growth rates at plus- and minus-ends were statistically significant with P<0.001 for all nucleotide mixtures except 0% GDP.
source: Using a two-sided t-test with unequal variance, differences in the mean normalized growth rates at plus- and minus-ends were statistically significant with P<0.001 for all nucleotide mixtures except 0% GDP.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 2 and represents statistical analysis of the data.
